[h1]Quakers Alive[/h1]

This game is so much fun, oh my god!

After the death of Unreal Tournament [spoiler](F#ck you Epic)[/spoiler], I've had to look for a new AFPS, and oh my god I've missed a good AFPS!

Really, my only problem with this game is that requires a lot of setting-up to do for it to run on modern systems. But I can overlook that, as whence that's done it runs & looks so beautifully! And it is also a mercifully short & easy process.



[h1] Run 'n' Gun! [/h1]

Hopping around these maps at 500 Km/s & turning the enemies' head into red glitter is so much fun!
Really, filling the enemy players with led & lasers never gets old!

The absolute insane movement you can do is insane, and the official & custom maps are so well-fit to be applicable with your inane dashing, letting them be open enough to let you jump around, yet also cramped enough to make you always within range to frag someone... it's [b]AMAZING!![/b]
And the movement is so simple, anyone can pick it up & run around like a freak within seconds; yet it craves a real pro to do such seamlessly. It's such a smooth & fun learning curve!

The weaponry in an AFPS game is essential to be any good, and Quake Live delivers!
The game's arsenal is huge! But not cramped to the point wherein you're overwhelmed. And I'm tired of modern-day multi-player FPS games & their balanced arsenals.
I want to feel good when picking up a good gun, I want to feel inherently better as soon as I find a good gun -- I enjoy fighting alongside everyone else in the server to overcome the guy with the good gun!
Really, I love this game's Deathmatch servers!... or Free For All, as it calls it. OK...



[h1] Community [/h1]

The community & playerbase of this game is so extremely kind & welcoming!
Really, it just seems the people that play AFPS games are inherently a lot kinder than any other multi-player games.
You can just hop into any server & hangout with the rest of the players in there. They're super accepting of newcomers & always willing to guide them with neat & niche tricks!

Also, the insane amount of variety of servers is awesome & amazing!
And there's always a handful of great servers constantly active!
Plus the sheer amount of community created fan content for this game is fantastic, by all these custom plugins & maps & commands & whatnot! It's freaking amazing & so much fun to f#ck around for a little while!



[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

I love this game so much!
It's a nice replacement of previous Unreal Tournament players -- it's akin but also individually unique!
I can't wait to play this game so much more in the future!

I overheard someone calling this game a "bastion of purity". I think that's a fitting description. It's like they assembled all of the best fps mechanic ideas and combined them into a meta without any distracting or diminishing features; just a pure fps game that puts the entire focus on the movement/gunplay/map control and strips out all the trivialities. The mixture of strafe/movement skill, item timing, and the mixture of tracking, hitscan, and prediction weapons makes it the perfect game to develop you as an FPS player. Anything played immediatley following it feels slow and casualized, and any time I return to it after not playing it for a while, it feels like a breath of fresh air. It's like an antidote for lootbox simulators/angle holders.

This is the game where I learned strafe jumping and all the other movements mechanics. I play it since 2009 and it's still the best PvP FPS. It's fast, very fast, it's brutal and merciless. I was getting destroyed when I started, but I sticked to it because the movements were mesmerizing, the sound effects amazing and the weapons balance perfect.

This is one of the games with the most amount of custom maps. There is a Race mode (defrag) and a Steam Workshop!

There are a few things to setup before starting (/com_idleSleep to have stable frame rate, /com_maxFPS 250 to increase the frame rate cap). The maps are colorful and vivid, the movements are absolutelly amazing and there is a ranking system (thanks to the Quake community for that). There is 2 main rulesets for movements, VQ3 and CPM/Turbo which has massive amount of air control. For Race mode I like both altough I prefer VQ3, for fighting modes I prefer VQ3 as the Turbo servers have fast weapons switch which I don't like.

I play it with max graphics settings and increased details + anisotropic filtering 16x and AA 8x forced in NVIDIA drivers.

If you are getting destroyed, you can join some servers which have level restriction based on Elo ranking (mainly FFA servers, some Clan Arena servers also), you can also try FreezeTag mode, or InstaGib/InstaFreeze. I suggest you try the Race mode, there are a TON of great maps. Don't be shy on asking for advices (there are people that will give you great combat skills advices).

If you are new to the game you can add me I'll tell you about the basics of Quake.

Hope this helps.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The game itself is awesome and smooth. I only use this game to train my aim/tracking, don't kill me for this. I've recently got into customizing it in my own dedicated server and you can basically create your custom modes and parameters. I don't think there's much need to discuss about the vanilla game, since, even though I could say many negative things (like RL being a bit too OP IMO), you can still customize everything in your own DS.

[h1]Technical stuff[/h1]
The id Tech engine in general has been an actual revolution regarding game engines. I'm going to review the technical side of the engine and point out many technical issues that mostly can't be fixed.
I'm reviewing them as a programmer, so regular users might not understand some of these. You've been warned.

[b]Questionable handling of the system timer[/b]
Let's say that the game can handle ordinary TSC timers pretty well, the same thing applies to standard ACPI timers. I can't say the same for HPET and the most recent TSC+ timers.
The engine skips some event frames when using HPET, recent TSC+ timers are mostly fine, except FPS Limiter behaving quite bad. Using HPET might also negatively affect your LG tracking, but this is not always the case.

[b]Very good overall programming of the engine[/b]
Expert programmers will indeed notice how the engine has been nicely programmed. Other than running fine on literally any PC (even toasters), this engine takes huge advantage from CPU extensions. Preventing this game from being affected by CPU mitigations will also increase performance a lot.

[b]Collisions move before models do[/b]
This is all about moving entities. One thing I've noticed is that player collisions (and entity collisions in general) move before models do. Experiencing rail rays going through player models without hitting are not rare at all.

[b]Nice mouse sampling algorithm[/b]
Nothing much to say here, the mouse sampling algorithm is actually really good compared to common standards.

[b]Incoherent framerate causes incoherent mouse movements[/b]
This is actually different than mouse sampling. The reliability of mouse movements is affected by incoherent framerate. If your framerate jumps a lot, your mouse movements will be affected as well. It is not rare at all to see your rail flicks fail when your framerate is jumping up and down. A good workaround is limiting your framerate so it is stable and static at a specific value. Use the [i]com_maxfps[/i] command.

[b]Ping issues related to timestamps[/b]
This is a common issue in most old game engines. It is really hard to explain how this issue works and it would take way too much time. There's basically a fixed amount of added latency (in ms) when DS startup timestamp and client startup timestamp differ from each others in some way.

Quake Live is a refined and enduring competitive first-person shooter that pays homage to the legacy of Quake III Arena while updating it for a new generation of players. Originally launched as a browser-based title and later migrating to Steam, Quake Live retains the blisteringly fast-paced gameplay, tight movement mechanics, and lethal precision that made its predecessor a staple of arena shooters. For veterans of the genre, it’s a near-perfect preservation of what made Quake III revolutionary. For newcomers, it's a crash course in a brutally unforgiving—but deeply rewarding—style of multiplayer combat that’s all but vanished in modern shooters.

At its core, Quake Live is about movement, map control, and raw skill. There are no loadouts, no leveling systems, and no unlockable weapons—every player starts on an even playing field. The difference lies in how you navigate the map, time item pickups, and win control over key areas. It’s a game that rewards practice and mastery above all else. The rocket jumps, strafe jumps, and circle strafing mechanics are integral to survival and dominance, and the learning curve is steep. But once you internalize these mechanics, the fluidity and speed at which you can move through maps becomes exhilarating.

Combat is intense, lightning-fast, and brutally precise. Unlike modern shooters that offer generous aim assists or slower pacing, Quake Live demands twitch reflexes and deep map knowledge. Every shot counts. Weapons are iconic and finely balanced—railguns for long-range precision, rocket launchers for splash damage, lightning guns for sustained duels. Mastery of weapon usage, coupled with smart item timing for health, armor, and powerups, forms the heart of competitive play. There's a constant mental calculation happening in high-level matches, and watching skilled players is like observing high-speed chess played with rocket launchers.

The game features a wide range of classic and community-created maps, many of which are meticulously designed for competitive play. Each map offers different dynamics, whether it’s verticality, tight corridors, or wide-open arenas. Modes like Duel, Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag, and Clan Arena cater to different styles of play, with Duel standing out as the purest test of one-on-one skill. Matches are often short, intense, and devoid of downtime, making the game highly addictive and mentally demanding.

Graphically, Quake Live is no longer cutting-edge, but its clean, readable aesthetic ensures that gameplay clarity always takes priority. The visuals may appear dated by modern standards, but the simplicity serves the competitive focus well—there’s no clutter, no visual noise, just pure, functional design. Sound design is equally crucial; directional audio cues are vital for tracking enemies and reacting to events in real time. The minimalist presentation allows for an experience that never distracts from the action.

One of the game’s major strengths is its tight community and the competitive culture that surrounds it. Quake Live has long been a training ground for some of the best FPS players in the world, and its esports history is rich with legendary rivalries and tournaments. However, this elite nature can be a double-edged sword. New players may find the skill gap daunting, especially without modern matchmaking systems to ease them in. The game’s learning curve, while satisfying for those who stick with it, is steep enough to deter casual players who expect more accessibility or progression-based incentives.

Over time, Quake Live has aged gracefully in terms of mechanics, but it faces challenges from a shrinking player base and the evolving tastes of the FPS genre. While newer titles prioritize persistent rewards, cosmetics, or expansive lore, Quake Live remains a purist’s dream—stripped down to its competitive essence. This uncompromising focus is admirable, but it also limits its mainstream appeal. It's a game built for people who love the process of getting better, who value mastery for its own sake, and who don't mind a lack of frills.

Ultimately, Quake Live is not just a throwback—it’s a living museum of arena FPS design, still functional, still exhilarating, and still capable of producing some of the most intense multiplayer experiences you can find. For players craving a shooter that prioritizes raw skill and moment-to-moment decision-making over loadouts and grinding, there is simply nothing else like it. Whether you’re returning to relive the glory days or discovering the roots of competitive FPS, Quake Live remains a benchmark for how refined and brutally beautiful a shooter can be.

Quake III Arena is a 1999 multiplayer-focused first-person shooter developed by "id Software". The third installment of the Quake series, Arena differs from previous games by excluding a story-based single-player mode and focusing primarily on multiplayer gameplay. The single-player mode is played against computer-controlled bots. It features music composed by Sonic Mayhem and Front Line Assembly founder Bill Leeb.

I have played Quake Live since 2010, back when it was a free plug-in for major browsers. I have also played Quake III Arena for longer, casually. 

Of course, nothing will beat the original Quake III Arena (Q3A) game, but this is a direct replacement for me. Instead of running a game from 1999 and using hacky methods to get it up to modern standards (native 16:9/16:10 resolution, HUD, etc), I just play this from now on. It includes many community fixes and has been supported for many years (and still is?) so that it looks the best it can be on modern systems. Plenty of bug fixes, too. The games only [b]real[/b] difference is the addition of a new weapon: the Heavy Machine Gun. It does not replace anything that I know of, but should be known. 

It still has that "boot up and frag 'em" mindset in that if you have a few minutes to kill, you can just get straight into a match with no bullshit, but is also flexible in the way that you can spend hours on it playing FFA, Clan Arena, Duel, CTF, FreezeTag and more! My personal favourite is Clan Arena :-) (There's a massive map pool, too!)

HOWEVER... This game can be plagued with fucking veterans. Some people on this have played since the dawn of Quake. They know all of the tricks in the book. Strafe jumping, rocket jumping, all that tomfoolery... So my recommendation to new players is: just stick to Free For All and Capture the Flag until you git gud. Clan Arena and Duels are the most likely to be riddled with these aforementioned skilled veterans. Best to stray away from that frustration. You will only end up abandoning the game like some of my friends have.

It used to be completely free with no subscriptions and extra stuff. It simply ran off advertisements. Apparently this was not enough for id software and decided to chuck in subscriptions. Then it was migrated to Steam as NPAPI plugins were no longer being supported on major browsers. Then you had to pay for the whole thing to phase out subscriptions and gain a more sure way of profit. No biggy, you essentially get the most definitive shooter of all time for £6.99. Bargain!

The players themselves are usually quite friendly, certainly not as bad as what can be found on CS:GO or any other modern shooter. Players from all over the world play it and you meet some of the best people.

[i]MODS MODS MODS[/i]... The closest thing you will get to mods are custom maps and some server side scripts. Type certain things into text chat and a sound plays. Class. You can get stuff from the Steam Workshop too, but nothing amazing. Maybe some "HD" models, and new extra player models which you cannot use in an online game, so pretty useless otherwise.

If you plan to buy this game, and you are new, I would recommend heading straight into the training arena bit (subject to change, name has changed throughout the years) and get yourself acquainted with the basics. Watch some videos on it. Give yourself the best headstart before you dive in head first. Also, bear in mind it is STILL based off the graphics from Q3A, which was released in 1999. The graphics were ahead of its time in those days and most people only play it now for the gameplay.

All in all, it does not stand up to its original counterpart for obvious reasons, but it gets a solid 9/10. Sticks true to its roots, plays well on modern machines, pleases eSports fans, fun with friends, and includes original game modes. If you are a seasoned Q3A player, you might find some things that annoy you but all in all it is the same old same old, and if you are new to the series or have not played Q3A, you will find the experience difficult to start, but is still fun in its own right!

EDIT: I should also mention the "liveliness" of the game. Is it popular? No. Will you find the same player(s) in a server in the same week? Probably. It should be mentioned that whatever game mode you want to play, there will be a server or two that have enough players in. Do not let this hinder your initial thoughts though (however positive or negative) because there is [b][i]ALWAYS[/i][/b] a bunch of servers to play on that have a good amount of players on. Tip: When on the server browser, filter out the empty and full servers and you will pretty much always find a decent server to go into every time you log in!
